## Proof

**Setup and normalization.** Let $S = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i$. The inequality is homogeneous of degree 4 on both sides, so we may normalize $S = 1$. We then seek the maximum of
$$f(x) = \sum_{1 \le i \le j \le n} x_i x_j(x_i^2 + x_j^2)$$
over the simplex $\{x_i \ge 0,\ \sum x_i = 1\}$, and set $c$ equal to this maximum.

**Simplifying the sum.** Split the sum into diagonal ($i=j$) and off-diagonal ($i<j$) parts:
$$f = \sum_i 2x_i^4 + \sum_{i<j} x_i x_j(x_i^2+x_j^2).$$

For the off-diagonal part, observe the identity
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n x_i^3 x_j = \Bigl(\sum_i x_i^3\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_j x_j\Bigr) = \sum_i x_i^3 \quad (\text{since } S=1),$$
while also
$$\sum_{i,j} x_i^3 x_j = \sum_i x_i^4 + \sum_{i<j}(x_i^3 x_j + x_j^3 x_i).$$
Therefore
$$\sum_{i<j} x_i x_j(x_i^2+x_j^2) = \sum_{i<j}(x_i^3 x_j + x_j^3 x_i) = \sum_i x_i^3 - \sum_i x_i^4.$$

Substituting back,
$$f = 2\sum_i x_i^4 + \sum_i x_i^3 - \sum_i x_i^4 = \sum_i x_i^3 + \sum_i x_i^4.$$

So we must maximize $g(x) = \sum_i x_i^3 + \sum_i x_i^4$ on the standard simplex.

**Maximizing a convex function on the simplex.** Each map $t \mapsto t^3$ and $t \mapsto t^4$ is convex on $[0,\infty)$, so $g$ is convex. A convex function on a compact convex polytope attains its maximum at an extreme point: for any convex combination $x = \sum_k \lambda_k v_k$ of the vertices $v_k$,
$$g(x) \le \sum_k \lambda_k\, g(v_k) \le \max_k g(v_k).$$

The vertices of the simplex are $e^{(k)}$ (the $k$-th unit vector). At such a vertex,
$$g(e^{(k)}) = 1^3 + 1^4 = 2,$$
with all other coordinates contributing $0$. Hence
$$\max_{\sum x_i = 1,\ x_i\ge 0} g(x) = 2.$$

**Conclusion.** The maximum of $f$ (under $S=1$) is $2$, attained when one $x_i = S$ and all others are $0$. Returning to the original (unnormalized) variables, the sharp inequality is
$$\sum_{1 \le i \le j \le n} x_i x_j(x_i^2+x_j^2) \le 2\Bigl(\sum_i x_i\Bigr)^4.$$

The constant $2$ is best possible, since equality holds for $(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = (t,0,\ldots,0)$ with $t>0$:
$$\text{LHS} = 2t^4, \qquad \text{RHS} = 2t^4.$$

Therefore the smallest such constant is $\boxed{c = 2}$.
